$comment: gzip byte ceilings for dist javascript. Ratchet down as the skeleton matures; raising a budget requires review.

notes.spec: 5000 -> 5100 (v9.53): zod 3.25 -> 4.6.7, which closes GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5 (high: a constrained collection can exhaust memory while validating). Measured 4963 -> 5025 B gzip over both module formats, +62 B for a validator whose runtime layout changed under it. Two API changes arrived with it and both are in this package: `z.record` now requires a key schema, and `z.SafeParseReturnType` is `z.ZodSafeParseResult`. The third-party JSON Schema bridge was removed rather than kept, because it reads v3 node types and cannot describe a v4 schema at all; `chartIrJsonSchema` now calls zod's own `toJSONSchema`. That uncovered a published lie — the function declared draft 2020-12 in a line the spread below it overwrote, so every schema it has ever emitted was draft-07 while the source said otherwise, and its own test passed only because a default Ajv compiles draft-07. The declaration now comes from the generator, and the `$id` that consumers resolve is unchanged.
notes.devkit: 5400 -> 6400 (v9.14): the paired report gains the resolution of its own deltas — pairedResolution (Wald interval on the paired difference, the smallest difference the cases could detect at 80% power, and the rule of three when two arms never disagreed) plus casesForEffect, which turns an observed discordance rate into the number of cases a 2pp claim would need. Measured 5352 -> 6281 B gzip over both module formats: about 0.9 KB for a capability the report quotes on every comparison, priced here rather than absorbed silently. The package had 48 B of headroom, so no existing export was near its ceiling and none was removed to pay for this. 6400 -> 6900 (v9.22): the pairing became one function. `pairByOccurrence` returns the aligned pairs and the two leftovers so that `compareArms` and `strata.pairCases` fold over the same alignment — the divergence between them was a real defect: the two readers of one artifact counted 2 pairs where the other counted 3 on a split that repeats a question. Measured 6387 -> 6766 B gzip over both module formats: about 0.4 KB for an exported function and two exported types, which is the price of not keeping two definitions of the same concept. Reviewed as a capability rather than drift; no export was removed to pay for it, because the alternative was leaving the second definition in place. 6900 -> 7100 (v9.46): the tie flag. `majorityResult` now reports whether the winner's group is tied with another group of the same size, which is the one fact that separates "the vote decided" from "arrival order decided" on a three-candidate pool — the two states have the same winner and the same `agreement`, so no caller could tell them apart without recomputing the group sizes. It is what makes spending a selector call only on undecidable questions an implementable policy rather than a replay: on 600 dev questions the cross pool returned one result 447 times, two 137 times and three 16 times, and the 16 are the only cases the vote cannot settle — `vote-unless-tie` reads 383 against the vote's 380 and the selector's 378 for 16 selection calls instead of 600 (`tools/pool-replay.mjs`, which reproduces the vote arm on 600 of 600 cases). Measured 6766 -> 6953 B gzip over both module formats: 187 B for a boolean and the loop that sets it in the pass that already picks the winner. The first version counted the tying groups in a second pass for 29 B more; the merged loop is smaller and cannot disagree with the winner it describes. Reviewed as a capability rather than drift; no export was removed to pay for it, because the alternative is a leaver that prices the call per question when the question is not what the call is for.
notes.ai: 88000 -> 91000 (v9.54): `shipment.ts`, the gate that decides whether a better prompt is worth its price. The module is the missing owner of a transfer that had none: `recipe.ts` says which prompt ships and the arm table says which prompt won, and nothing compared a gain against the bill it is paid on — so the accuracy table's best cell (66.45% at 9.7x the tokens, p = 0.42) would have been applied by any rule that read one column. Measured 88,000 -> 90,631 B gzip over both module formats (+2,631 B, 2.9%): the six-field evidence record, the arithmetic closure that refuses a declaration whose paired halves disagree, the tariff that turns two metrics into one comparison, and the chain fold CI holds to `resolveShipment`. Nothing was moved out to pay for it: the exact McNemar tail and the paired interval stay in `devkit` and are handed in, because a second implementation of a statistic inside the product would be a second opinion about what a reading means. Earlier: 85000 -> 88000 (v9.49): two procedures and a generator. `template.ts` gains a shape table so a template is one row rather than a second renderer (the three that exist differ in one sentence pair and in where their worked examples come from), and `examples.ts` is new: the prompt that writes question-SQL pairs for one database and the parser that reads the reply. Measured 84,489 -> 87,672 B gzip over both module formats, +3,183 B for a module a customer can run (the prompt and the parser both live here; only the cache is in the harness). No export was removed to pay for it and no existing module changed size by more than a line, so the increment is the feature rather than drift. 91000 -> 95000 (v9.55): the domain reader and the statement shape it resolves against. `sql-lex.ts` is the scanner that answers "which table does `t1.status` mean" — moved out of `eval/bird/statement.ts`, not copied, because `ask_question` now has to answer it for a customer's own database and two scanners would agree on the easy statements and disagree on the ones with a CTE, a quoted identifier or a `from` inside a literal. `domain.ts` is the lookup the grounding rewrite needs: `createDomainReader` reads one column's distinct values through any runner, `createGroundingReader` resolves the statement's own aliases first. Measured 90631 -> 94420 B gzip over both module formats (+3,789 B, 4.2%). Nothing was moved out to pay for it and the harness shrank by the same code: `eval/bird/statement.ts` went from 593 lines to 432, and its `createDomainReader` is now a two-line wrapper over this one. The alternative was a second implementation of a rule whose whole licence is the set of values it compares against — and the move already found one defect in the version that shipped inside the harness: `String(null)` turned the NULL group into the four-character spelling `null`, which a nullable column then offered as a value it does not contain.
notes.node: 17000 -> 18000 (v9.37): cancellation that reaches the server. `pg` does not cancel a statement it has already sent, so the connector's forwarded `AbortSignal` was a comment that looked like a guarantee: aborting during `select pg_sleep(1)` returned the row a second later. The fix learns each physical connection's `pg_backend_pid()` once, asks the server to `pg_cancel_backend` it on a connection of its own when the caller aborts, destroys the connection instead of recycling a half-read protocol, and maps SQLSTATE 57014 (both our cancel and the server's own `statement_timeout`) to `NL2C_E_TIMEOUT`. Measured 16726 -> 17261 B gzip over both module formats: 535 B for the only path that makes a deadline a deadline. A capability, priced here rather than absorbed silently; no export was removed to pay for it, because the alternative is a signal that silently does nothing.
notes.core: 36000 -> 40000 (v9.38): the query-intent renderer and its expression grammar. `packages/core/src/semantic/intent.ts` turns a JSON query description into a statement — tables, join column pairs, filters as (column, op, value) triples including ranges, grain, order — with three rules that are the reason it is a compiler and not a prompt: identifiers are validated instead of quoted (a double-quoted token that names no column is read as a string literal by SQLite, so escaping fails silently on the engine this benchmark runs), literals are rendered from values, and expressions are tokenised and parsed. The parser is most of the weight: a five-level grammar (or / and / one comparison / concat and +- / */ with function calls, parentheses, searched and simple CASE) plus the sixteen-name refusal vocabulary the harness reads as data. Measured 30187 -> 39561 B gzip over both module formats: 9,374 B for the only code in this repository that can remove a class of statement defects instead of redistributing them. A capability, priced here rather than absorbed silently; no export was removed to pay for it, because the alternative was leaving 'the model wrote it badly' as an explanation with no instrument under it. 40000 -> 42000 (v9.39): quoting, and the schema check that quoting makes mandatory. The first probe refused 10 of 40 replies and the histogram said why: `bad-identifier` cannot be answered by a bare-word lexer when the corpus spells columns `County Name` and `Charter School (Y/N)`, which is 4.6% of the columns in BIRD's own databases. Names are now checked for what cannot appear in one and quoted when a bare word would not survive, in filters, joins, group-by keys and inside expressions (where a double-quoted token is a name and a single-quoted one is a string). Quoting is what then makes the column list load-bearing — SQLite reads a double-quoted token that names no column as a string literal — so `compileIntent` takes the schema and refuses `unknown-identifier`, which is a seventeenth refusal name and one more branch on the funnel. Measured 39561 -> 41403 B gzip over both module formats: 1,842 B for the difference between a grammar that excludes a sixth of one database's vocabulary and one that does not. 42000 -> 43000 (v9.40): what the second probe's twelve refusals asked for, read one at a time. Operators are matched without case (`IS NULL` is one predicate, not a spelling), a `null` value on the nullary ones is read as a missing value, a scalar on `in` is the one-element list it means, a filter's left side may be an expression under its own key (so `HAVING count(p.Id) > 5` is expressible, which `column` could not carry — a column name may itself contain a space and a parenthesis), a select alias is a name the statement invents and is no longer looked up in the schema, and a tokenizer that used to read `f."School Name"` as a bare name plus a stray dot now reads it as one reference. Measured 41403 -> 42168 B gzip over both module formats: 765 B, and the six changes between them account for nine of the twelve refusals a 120-question probe produced — the difference between reading what a model wrote and grading its vocabulary.
notes.mcp: 7000 -> 10500: the server gained the one tool the project is named for. `ask_question` runs the question-to-SQL pipeline and returns the statement with its rows, which means `mcp` now depends on `ai` — an edge the layering rule already permits (ai depends only on core and spec) and that no package used until now, which is why a server could run SQL and could not answer a question. Measured 6,500 -> 9,518 B gzip (+3,018) over both module formats: the tree-shaken pipeline, the schema validator and the tool definition. The alternative was to put the generation in the client, and then every MCP consumer would reimplement the guard, the repair loop and the empty-result turn — four mechanisms this package would then be unable to measure. The tool is listed only when a provider is configured, so a server with no key ships the same bytes the budget was set for and answers three tools. 10500 -> 11500 (v9.55): the shipped domain read. `ask_question` now hands the pipeline the reader that was priced on BIRD — 14 repairs and no losses on dev, 7 through the gated form — so the rule stops being a harness-only capability. About 0.8 KB gzip over both module formats for the reader over the caller's runner, the cap that turns an unfinished read into a refusal (1,000 distinct values, reported by the runner as `truncated`), and the `grounding` field in the payload, which is what lets a deployment see whether the rule fired at all. Reviewed as a capability rather than drift: the alternative is a product that cannot tell a database where every spelling was already right from one where every read failed.
notes.chart: 37900 -> 39200 (v9.50): the matrix limit. `toChartIR`'s `limit` sliced rows, so a heatmap whose column did not fit was cut inside it and the remainder read as missing data — the one reading a heatmap exists to give. The fix adds `matrixFieldOf` (what a matrix is, read off the encoding) and `wholeColumns` (the limit in columns, with a refusal when one column does not fit), about 0.9 KB gzip over both module formats: measured 38792 B, which is 892 B over the old ceiling. Reviewed as a capability rather than drift. The two docstrings were tightened before this number was taken and the figure did not move, so the growth is code and not prose. No export was removed to pay for it: the alternative was a library that draws half a lane, which no test would have caught from a label. 39200 -> 41000 (v9.52): the histogram reading. A question that names a histogram is answered by pooling the table's finite numbers and counting them into equal-width bins, which needs `pooledDistribution` (the binning rule, its two clamps and the label a bin states), `histogramReading` (which columns are pooled, and the two field names it invents around a table that already uses them) and `binnedIR` (the encoding and the alt text a binned bar owes a screen reader). Measured 40905 B, which is 1705 B over the old ceiling: about 1.7 KB gzip for ~120 lines, and the docstrings were shortened first and the figure did not move by a byte, which proves the growth is code and not prose — comments are stripped from dist. Reviewed as a capability rather than as drift: the alternative was to keep 90 corpus rows unreachable so the bundle could stay under a number that nobody outside this repository reads.
